TL;DR
An Edge AI platform is an end-to-end engineering system: data ingestion, feature engineering, inference, monitoring, and human workflows must all hold together. The design uses five layers: React/MUI presentation, Flask APIs, analytics, edge execution, and SQLite/file persistence. A bounded deque batches recent samples (for example, 500 records or about five seconds) before feature extraction; it is a buffer, not a durable queue. PHM combines signal features (RMS, FFT), One-Class SVM, DTW, and PCA drift monitoring, with interpretation left to engineers. AI agents are controlled application clients: the backend enforces tool allowlists, authorization, validation, and audit logging, not the LLM prompt. Deployment starts as a Docker Compose edge monolith and should scale to decoupled workers only when measurements justify it. Bottom line: Reliability comes from traceable data, explicit failure behavior, and governed agents — not from a single model or framework.
Building an Edge AI platform is not just about deploying a machine-learning model close to a machine. In a semiconductor manufacturing environment, the platform must connect sensor data, feature engineering, model inference, health monitoring, user workflows, and maintenance decisions into a system that can be operated and maintained reliably.
This article introduces an Edge AI / Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) platform from a system-design perspective. It covers the architecture, data flow, analytical methods, backend implementation, AI-agent integration, deployment, failure handling, and the trade-offs behind the design.
The emphasis is on how the components work together — not simply on listing technologies.
1. Project Overview The platform is designed to turn equipment signals into information that engineers can use to investigate equipment health and plan maintenance. Its main workflow can be summarized as:
flowchart LR A[Sensor Data] --> B[Feature Engineering] B --> C[ML Analysis] C --> D[Edge Inference] D --> E[Health Monitoring] E --> F[AI Agent] F --> G[Engineering Decision]At a high level, the platform provides four capabilities:
Capability Purpose Sensor-data processing Collect, organize, and transform equipment signals into usable data Feature engineering and ML Extract signal characteristics, identify unusual patterns, and support health assessment Health monitoring Track health scores, historical changes, and potential abnormal conditions AI-assisted workflows Retrieve relevant data, summarize findings, and help engineers investigate the next step The AI agent is an assistance layer, not an autonomous replacement for engineering judgment. Decisions that can affect production equipment should remain subject to appropriate validation and human oversight.
2. Why Edge AI? A model is only one part of a production system. The surrounding data path, deployment process, integration points, and operational controls often determine whether an AI solution is useful in practice.
2.1 Common engineering challenges Integration complexity. Data acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, APIs, dashboards, and alerts may be implemented by different components. Without clear interfaces, even a small change can require updates across multiple modules.
Data lineage. Engineers need to understand where a feature or score came from, which source data was used, and which model or configuration produced the result. Without traceability, it is difficult to reproduce an analysis or compare results over time.
Deployment latency. A solution that works in a development environment can still be difficult to package, configure, install, and update consistently at an equipment site.
2.2 The intended improvement The platform aims to standardize the path from data ingestion to operational use.
Engineering area Intended outcome Deployment Reduce the effort required to package and release a platform update Integration Reuse common interfaces instead of repeatedly writing project-specific integration code Data lineage Make analysis inputs, outputs, and model versions easier to trace Maintenance workflow Present data and analysis in a form that supports investigation and follow-up The project materials include illustrative figures such as a deployment cycle reduced from 28 days to 1 day, an 85% reduction in integration code, and 100% synchronization of data lineage within the measured scope. These numbers should be published as verified results only if their definitions, measurement periods, and comparison baselines can be documented. Otherwise, label them as internal estimates or targets.
3. System Architecture The platform can be understood as five cooperating layers: presentation, API services, analytics, edge execution, and persistence.
flowchart TB subgraph UI["Presentation Layer"] A["React + MUI"] B["Workflow UI / React Flow"] end subgraph API["API and Application Layer"] C["Flask REST APIs"] D["Authentication and Job Coordination"] end subgraph ML["Analytics Layer"] E["Feature Engineering"] F["ML / PHM Algorithms"] G["Health Score and Drift Analysis"] end subgraph EDGE["Edge Execution Layer"] H["Sensor / File Inputs"] I["Edge Runtime and Inference"] end subgraph DATA["Persistence Layer"] J["edge_ai.db"] K["vibration.db"] L["Model and Analysis Artifacts"] end A --> C B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G H --> I I --> E D --> J E --> K F --> L3.1 Presentation layer The web interface uses React and Material UI (MUI) to present equipment information, analysis results, and operational workflows. React Flow can be used to represent workflows or agent execution paths visually.
The frontend should focus on user interaction and presentation. It should not become the source of truth for model execution, access control, or data integrity.
3.2 API and application layer The Flask backend exposes REST APIs and coordinates application-level operations, such as authentication, analysis requests, data retrieval, and report generation.
Keeping these responsibilities behind a stable API allows the frontend, analysis modules, and edge processes to evolve without requiring every component to know the implementation details of the others.
3.3 Analytics layer This layer contains signal processing, feature extraction, anomaly detection, health scoring, and data-drift analysis. It should expose well-defined inputs and outputs so that algorithms can be tested independently from the web application.
3.4 Edge execution layer The edge runtime handles local execution and interaction with the available sensor-data sources. Local processing can reduce dependence on continuous network connectivity and avoid sending every high-frequency raw sample to a central service.
The exact division between local and centralized processing depends on latency, compute resources, network reliability, data volume, and deployment constraints.
3.5 Persistence layer The current design uses SQLite databases for application and vibration-related data, along with files for model or analysis artifacts. This is a pragmatic starting point for a local or single-node deployment, but it introduces concurrency and lifecycle considerations as workload grows.
4. End-to-End Data Flow A typical processing path consists of ingestion, buffering, persistence, feature extraction, model analysis, health assessment, and follow-up action.
flowchart TD A["Sensor / File Input"] --> B["In-Memory Buffer"] B --> C{"Batch Trigger"} C -->|"Time or size threshold"| D["Persist / Prepare Batch"] D --> E["Feature Extraction"] E --> F["ML / PHM Analysis"] F --> G["Health Score and Anomaly Results"] G --> H["Dashboard / Report / Alert"] H --> I["Engineer Review and Action"]4.1 Buffering and batching A bounded Python deque, for example deque(maxlen=5000), can be used to hold recent samples before processing. A batch may be triggered by a time interval (for example, approximately five seconds) or a record-count threshold (for example, 500 records), depending on the implementation.
A bounded deque automatically discards the oldest entries when it reaches capacity. It is therefore a useful short-term buffer, but it is not a durable message queue. If samples must survive process crashes or temporary downstream failures, the system needs an explicit persistence and replay strategy.
flowchart LR A["Sensor Stream"] --> B["Bounded In-Memory Queue"] B --> C["Batch Flush Worker"] C --> D["SQLite Persistence"]4.2 Feature extraction and analysis The batch is transformed into signal features and passed to the relevant analytical methods. The output may include feature values, anomaly indicators, a health score, and supporting metadata.
4.3 Results and action The platform presents results through dashboards, reports, or alerts. The purpose is not merely to generate a score; it is to give engineers enough context to inspect the evidence, understand the potential issue, and decide what to do next.
5. Machine Learning and PHM Methods PHM systems combine domain knowledge, signal processing, statistical analysis, and machine learning. No single algorithm can reliably answer every equipment-health question.
5.1 Signal features Common time-domain features include:
RMS (root mean square): summarizes signal magnitude and is often used to monitor vibration energy. Peak: captures the largest absolute amplitude in a window. Kurtosis: describes aspects of a distribution’s tail behavior and can help identify impulsive signals. Its interpretation depends on the data distribution and implementation. FFT (Fast Fourier Transform): transforms a time-domain signal into frequency-domain components, helping reveal dominant frequencies and changes in spectral structure. For a signal \(x = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N]\), RMS is defined as:
$$ \mathrm{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2} $$Feature definitions, window sizes, sampling rates, units, and preprocessing should be consistent. Otherwise, apparent changes may come from the pipeline rather than the equipment.
5.2 One-Class SVM for anomaly detection One-Class Support Vector Machine (One-Class SVM) can learn the boundary of data considered normal and flag observations that fall outside that boundary. It is useful when labeled fault examples are limited.
Important considerations include:
Fit the model on a representative baseline of normal operation. Scale features consistently. Tune parameters such as nu and gamma using validation data and operational feedback. Monitor false positives and false negatives; an anomaly score is not automatically a diagnosis. Revisit the baseline when operating conditions or equipment configurations change. flowchart LR A["Historical Normal Data"] --> B["Feature Scaling"] B --> C["Train One-Class SVM"] C --> D["Learn Decision Boundary"] D --> E["New Feature Vector: Normal or Anomaly"]5.3 Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) Dynamic Time Warping measures similarity between sequences that may differ in timing or duration. It can be useful when comparing signal patterns whose important events do not occur at exactly the same time.
A DTW implementation uses a cumulative-cost matrix. A typical recurrence is:
$$ D(i,j) = d(x_i,y_j) + \min\left\{ D(i-1,j),\; D(i,j-1),\; D(i-1,j-1) \right\} $$where \(d(x_i,y_j)\) is the local distance between two points. Constraints such as a warping window can reduce computation and prevent implausible alignments. DTW is not a universal anomaly detector; its usefulness depends on the selected reference sequences, distance function, normalization, and domain.
5.4 PCA for data-drift monitoring Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects correlated features into a lower-dimensional space. Comparing current data with a reference baseline can help identify distribution changes.
A drift signal does not necessarily mean equipment failure. It may also reflect a changed recipe, sensor replacement, a different operating regime, or a preprocessing change. Drift should trigger investigation and contextual checks rather than an automatic conclusion.
flowchart LR A["Historical Baseline Features"] --> B["Fit PCA Model"] B --> C["Reference Feature Space"] C --> D["New Features: Projection and Drift Analysis"]5.5 Choosing the method Method Primary purpose Key limitation RMS / Peak / Kurtosis Summarize time-domain signal characteristics Can be sensitive to windowing, noise, and operating conditions FFT Identify spectral components and frequency changes Requires appropriate sampling and interpretation One-Class SVM Detect deviations from a learned normal-data boundary Depends on baseline quality and parameter selection DTW Compare sequences with temporal misalignment Can be computationally expensive and reference-dependent PCA Monitor multivariate structure and potential drift Drift is not equivalent to failure A robust PHM workflow combines these methods with engineering context, historical evidence, and validation.
6. Backend Design 6.1 Flask application structure Flask Blueprints can separate API areas by responsibility — for example, authentication, equipment data, analysis, reports, and agent operations. This makes the application easier to test and maintain than a single large route module.
The backend should validate request parameters, enforce authorization, handle errors consistently, and return predictable response formats. Long-running analysis should be treated differently from short synchronous API requests.
6.2 Authentication and authorization The platform uses LDAP / Active Directory integration for organizational identity and JWTs for authenticated requests, according to the implementation design.
These mechanisms serve different purposes: directory authentication verifies a user’s identity, while a token can carry authenticated-session claims to subsequent API calls. Authorization still needs to be checked for each protected operation. Tokens should have appropriate expiry and signing configuration, and secrets must not be hard-coded into source code or container images.
flowchart LR A["User Login"] --> B["LDAP / AD Authentication"] B --> C["Issue JWT Access Token"] C --> D["Authorized API Requests"] D --> E["Backend Permission Checks"]6.3 SQLite and data separation The design separates application data and vibration data into two SQLite databases, such as:
edge_ai.db — application records, configuration, and workflow-related information. vibration.db — vibration-related data and analysis inputs. SQLAlchemy can manage database interactions, and SQLite’s ATTACH DATABASE feature can support selected cross-database queries. However, separate database files do not remove all consistency or concurrency concerns. Cross-database operations, transaction boundaries, backups, schema migrations, and recovery procedures need explicit testing.
SQLite is suitable for many local deployments. If concurrent writes or multi-node access become substantial, a client-server database such as PostgreSQL may be a more appropriate next step.
6.4 Scheduled tasks and model history APScheduler can run periodic jobs such as drift checks, report generation, or maintenance summaries. The job should be designed to tolerate retries, failures, and partial completion.
One important deployment detail: starting the scheduler in multiple web-worker processes can cause the same job to run more than once unless scheduling is coordinated. For multi-process deployments, consider a dedicated scheduler process or another mechanism that ensures a single active job owner.
Model-build history should record enough metadata to reproduce an analysis, such as model version, training-data reference, configuration, creation time, and evaluation results. The exact fields depend on the platform’s traceability requirements.
A build also needs explicit states, so that a failed run is distinguishable from one that never started:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> building building --> completed building --> failed7. AI Agent: From Data Retrieval to Assisted Investigation An AI agent can help users navigate the platform by translating a natural-language request into a controlled sequence of data retrieval and analysis operations. The LLM should not be the only component responsible for correctness or security.
flowchart TD A["User Request"] --> B["LLM Planner / Orchestrator"] B --> C["Select an Approved Tool"] C --> D["Backend Validation and Authorization"] D --> E["Execute Tool"] E --> F["Structured Result"] F --> G{"More Evidence Needed?"} G -->|"Yes"| B G -->|"No"| H["LLM Summary"] H --> I["Response / Report for Human Review"]7.1 Example tools Depending on the actual deployment, the agent may expose tools such as:
Tool Responsibility get_health_score Retrieve a health score and its relevant context get_vibration_data Fetch authorized vibration data for a specified asset or time range run_sql_query_safe Execute a constrained, read-only query against approved data anomaly_detection Run a defined anomaly-analysis workflow read_file Read permitted files from an allowlisted location export_report Generate a report using validated inputs Tool names are illustrative; document only tools that are implemented and available in the deployed version.
7.2 Tool governance and safety The model should propose an action, but the backend should enforce the rules. At minimum:
Validate arguments against a schema. Authenticate the user and authorize access to the requested asset and data. Use allowlists for files, tools, and queryable resources. Restrict database operations; do not allow arbitrary destructive SQL. Apply timeouts, output-size limits, and audit logging. Return structured errors that the agent can handle without exposing secrets. Require explicit confirmation for consequential actions where appropriate. A prompt instruction alone is not a security boundary. Enforcement belongs in the application and tool implementation.
7.3 Separate planning from execution One possible design uses a larger model for high-level planning and a smaller model for tool-oriented execution. For example, a planner model can break a request into subtasks, while an executor selects from approved tools and handles structured results.
This split can help separate reasoning from action execution, but it also adds orchestration complexity, latency, and more failure points. It should be evaluated against a simpler single-model or deterministic workflow rather than assumed to be better by default.
7.4 Server-Sent Events (SSE) Server-Sent Events can stream progress or partial results from the backend to the frontend over an HTTP connection. This is useful when an agent performs multiple steps and the user should see that work is progressing.
The implementation should define event types, error behavior, connection timeouts, and client reconnection semantics. Streaming text to the interface does not replace backend logging or durable job state.
8. Deployment and Observability 8.1 Docker Compose Docker Compose can package the web application and its supporting services for repeatable deployment on a single host. It helps standardize runtime dependencies, ports, environment variables, volumes, and startup relationships.
A container being healthy does not guarantee that the whole application is functioning correctly. Readiness checks should verify the dependencies that matter, and persistent data should be stored in appropriate volumes rather than only in a container’s writable layer.
8.2 Runtime frontend configuration If the frontend needs to be deployed as a static bundle whose backend URL can change by environment, a runtime configuration file such as env.js can expose a value through window.ENV. This avoids rebuilding the frontend bundle for every deployment environment.
The runtime configuration must be loaded before application code reads it, validated at startup, and treated as public configuration. Do not put passwords, API secrets, or other credentials in browser-visible variables.
flowchart LR A["Docker Image"] --> B["Container Entrypoint"] B --> C["Runtime Environment Variables"] C --> D["env.js"] D --> E["window.ENV"] E --> F["Frontend API Endpoint"]8.3 Monitoring Useful operational signals include:
API request rate, latency, and error rate. Data-ingestion delay, batch size, and dropped-sample counts. Model execution duration and analysis failures. Scheduler job start time, duration, and outcome. Agent tool-call success rate, timeouts, and token or inference cost where available. Disk usage, database growth, and artifact-storage health. Observability should help answer three questions: what failed, where it failed, and whether the system can safely recover.
9. Failure Handling and Scaling Failure handling should be designed into the data path, rather than added only after an incident.
Failure scenario Risk Possible mitigation Buffer reaches capacity Old samples may be discarded Track overflow/drop counts; use durable buffering if loss is unacceptable Sensor or source becomes unavailable Incomplete or stale analysis Track freshness, surface missing-data status, and avoid treating stale values as current Model execution fails Missing or invalid result Record failure context, apply bounded retries, and preserve the previous valid result with a clear timestamp SQLite write contention Delayed or failed writes Reduce competing writers, batch writes, tune transactions, or migrate to a server database Scheduled task runs twice Duplicate reports or work Use a single scheduler owner, idempotent jobs, or a distributed coordination mechanism LLM or tool call times out Incomplete agent workflow Apply timeouts, bounded retries, structured error handling, and a user-visible partial/failure state Network connectivity is interrupted Remote service unavailable Keep appropriate local capabilities, queue recoverable work, and define synchronization behavior 9.1 Evolve in stages Scaling should respond to measured constraints, not to technology fashion.
flowchart LR A["Stage 1: Edge Monolith"] --> B["Stage 2: Decoupled Pipeline"] B --> C["Stage 3: Cloud / Multi-Node Scale-Out"]Stage 1 — Edge monolith. A compact Flask application, local persistence, and local inference can be effective for a single-node deployment with modest workload.
Stage 2 — Decoupled pipeline. When ingestion and analysis interfere with API responsiveness, introduce durable queues and separate workers. This makes retries and backpressure easier to control.
Stage 3 — Cloud or multi-node scale-out. When workload, availability, or concurrent access demands it, consider a client-server database, shared job coordination, centralized observability, and horizontally scalable services. The edge component can remain responsible for latency-sensitive local functions.
Potential technologies such as MQTT, durable message brokers, Redis, PostgreSQL, and load balancers are options for future evolution — not proof that the current deployment already uses them.
flowchart LR A["Sensors / Edge Devices"] --> B["MQTT Broker"] B --> C["Durable Message Queue"] C --> D["Worker Cluster"] D --> E["ML Inference"] D --> F["PostgreSQL"] D --> G["Redis Cache"] E --> H["Flask API"] F --> H G --> H H --> I["Frontend"]10. Engineering Trade-offs Every architecture reflects constraints. The objective is not to select the most sophisticated technology in every layer, but to make the current system reliable while preserving a practical path forward.
Area Current approach Benefit Trade-off / next consideration Web backend Flask Lightweight and straightforward to organize Long-running tasks may need separate workers Persistence SQLite Simple local deployment and low operational overhead Concurrent writes and multi-node access are limited Scheduling APScheduler Convenient for periodic jobs Multi-process execution needs coordination Data buffering Bounded deque Fast and simple in-memory buffering Not durable; old entries are discarded at capacity Frontend updates REST APIs and SSE Familiar request-response model with optional streaming Reconnection and job state must be designed ML / PHM Feature engineering plus multiple analytical methods Combines interpretable signal features with statistical and ML methods Requires baseline validation and domain-specific interpretation Deployment Docker Compose Repeatable single-host deployment Not a complete orchestration solution for large clusters A useful engineering principle is to separate what exists today from what may be introduced later. This distinction makes the design easier to review and prevents a roadmap from being mistaken for a production capability.
11. Conclusion An Edge AI platform is an end-to-end engineering system. Its value comes from connecting sensor data, signal processing, model execution, backend services, deployment, monitoring, and human workflows into a coherent operational path.
The main lessons are:
Design the complete data path. A model is useful only when its inputs, outputs, errors, and operational context are handled reliably. Make data and results traceable. Versioning and lineage are essential for debugging and comparing analyses. Treat AI agents as controlled application clients. The backend — not the LLM prompt — must enforce permissions, validation, and tool safety. Make failure behavior explicit. Buffers, schedulers, databases, network dependencies, and model calls all need defined failure semantics. Scale based on evidence. Begin with a design that matches the deployment constraints, then decouple or replace components when measurements justify the change. The most valuable work is often not a single algorithm or framework. It is the engineering judgment required to make the components work together safely, predictably, and maintainably.
Terms of use: This article is written for technical exchange and system-design discussion. Identifying information about companies, customers and internal projects has been removed, and the data and scenarios have been de-identified or virtualized. The architectures described as future evolution are possible directions, not claims that all of them have been implemented or deployed. The use and redistribution of the text and diagrams follows the licensing terms published by the author.

title: Designing a Semiconductor Equipment Edge AI Platform: From Sensor Data to Intelligent Decisions

content:
TL;DR
The architecture spans six layers, from sensors and streaming through PHM, edge agents, and MES/EAP safety integration. A 20-machine, 3-channel, 2 kHz example generates about 41.5 GB/day of raw data; managed fleet size and high-frequency stream scale are separate metrics. Detection uses a two-stage pipeline: Isolation Forest screening followed by Autoencoder assessment, with alert consolidation to reduce noise. RUL prediction (Weibull, LSTM/Transformer, domain features) feeds 30-day and 7-day maintenance planning; the reported figures are project-specific, not universal benchmarks. Models move through standardized packaging, shadow deployment, canary rollout (5% → 20% → 100%), monitoring, and rollback. Edge Agents, Industrial RAG, and MLOps connect evidence and workflows, but safety-critical control stays outside the LLM. Bottom line: Make each layer observable, verifiable, and recoverable before expanding autonomous decision-making.
Introduction This article documents the Smart Fab Edge AI system architecture I presented in an interview presentation, expanding the original 11-slide deck into a more comprehensive technical reference.
Starting with equipment sensor data, the article walks through real-time data processing, anomaly detection, Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction, edge deployment, industrial knowledge retrieval, and the decision-making capabilities and control boundaries of AI agents. Beyond the technical components, it discusses the design considerations at each layer and the trade-offs among latency, computational resources, reliability, and operational maintenance costs.
The central challenge is not simply deploying AI models in a factory. It is designing a system that can operate continuously under constrained computing resources while integrating with existing equipment controls, maintenance workflows, and factory information systems.
The equipment scale and selected performance figures described in this article are drawn from previous project experience and interview materials. Information concerning companies, customers, equipment configurations, and internal systems has been anonymized or generalized. Because some original test records are no longer available, the performance figures presented here are not claimed to have undergone independent revalidation. Readers should interpret each metric according to its definition and scope rather than treating it as an industry benchmark applicable to every factory.
Intellectual Property and Usage Notice: This article is intended for technical knowledge sharing, system architecture discussions, and demonstration of personal technical capabilities. The content has been anonymized and adjusted where necessary. It should not contain confidential customer data, trade secrets, or non-public internal project information. The use and redistribution of the text and diagrams are subject to the licensing terms published by the author.
01. System Objectives and Design Assumptions Production lines in semiconductor manufacturing share several operational characteristics: a wide variety of equipment, high-frequency sensor data, substantial downtime costs, and control processes with strict latency and reliability requirements.
Sending all data to the cloud for centralized analysis and decision-making can simplify management. However, it also increases network transmission overhead, data governance complexity, and system dependencies. This architecture therefore combines edge computing with centralized management, keeping latency-sensitive processing within the factory.
The overall design focuses on four key considerations:
Data governance and security: Sensor data, equipment information, and maintenance records are handled according to data classification and access control policies. Sensitive data should, in principle, undergo necessary processing and management within the factory. Cross-system data transfers must comply with internal security requirements. Edge computing resources: Model size, inference frequency, and buffering strategies are selected according to the available CPU, memory, and accelerator resources of each edge device. Anomaly detection usability: Model accuracy alone is insufficient. False-positive rates, false-negative rates, alert frequency, and the resulting workload for on-site personnel must also be evaluated. Equipment safety and fault isolation: AI models can provide anomaly assessments and maintenance recommendations, but safety-critical control logic must remain under the responsibility of validated control systems and established safety mechanisms. These assumptions directly influence the subsequent architectural layers, model selection, and permission design for AI agents.
02. End-to-End Technical Architecture The overall architecture consists of six layers. The sensing and data acquisition layer captures equipment status, while the streaming and signal processing layers organize and transform incoming data. The AI analytics layer performs anomaly detection and health assessment. The upper layers coordinate decisions, maintenance workflows, and the necessary control interfaces.
Layer Name Key Technologies and Responsibilities 01 Sensing and Data Acquisition MCUs, IO-Link, vibration/current/pressure sensors 02 Streaming and Time-Series Data Kafka, InfluxDB, ring buffers, timestamps, and synchronization 03 Signal Processing FFT, wavelet transforms, time-domain and frequency-domain feature extraction 04 AI Analytics and PHM Isolation Forest, Autoencoders, LSTM/Transformer, and RUL prediction 05 Edge Agent and Task Orchestration State management, tool routing, workflow orchestration, and model selection 06 Integration and Safety Control SECS/GEM, MES/EAP APIs, authorization, and safety middleware Within this architecture, edge devices primarily handle low-latency data processing and inference. The centralized platform manages models, performs cross-equipment analytics and training, and coordinates model deployment.
Responsibilities must also be clearly separated among individual components. Kafka is suitable for message delivery and decoupling data streams. InfluxDB supports time-series storage and querying. Ring buffers are useful for continuous data processing with predictable memory consumption.
These components do not necessarily need to be connected in a single linear pipeline. Their actual combination depends on data frequency, latency requirements, and the deployment environment.
Similarly, edge inference and equipment control are not the same thing. Even if a model produces a result within a few milliseconds, end-to-end latency must account for data acquisition, signal processing, inference, communication, and controller execution time.
03. High-Throughput Data Streaming and Signal Processing In high-frequency sensing scenarios, the first challenge is often not model accuracy but how to process a continuous stream of incoming data efficiently.
Data Volume Estimation and Scope Consider a representative data scenario with 20 machines, each equipped with three sensor channels. Each channel continuously samples at 2 kHz, and each sample is stored as a 4-byte value.
The raw numerical data generated per second is:
$$ 20 \times 3 \times 2{,}000 \times 4 = 480{,}000\ \text{bytes/s} $$The corresponding daily data volume is:
$$ 480{,}000 \times 86{,}400 = 41{,}472{,}000{,}000\ \text{bytes/day} $$This is approximately 41.47 GB per day, using decimal units where 1 GB = \(10^9\) bytes.
This estimate includes only the raw sensor values. It excludes timestamps, communication packet overhead, indexes, database storage formats, and other metadata. Once these additional overheads are included, actual transmission or storage requirements could approach 50 GB per day, depending on the data format and system design.
The 20-machine scenario is an illustrative calculation, not a statement that the entire system manages only 20 machines. Nor should this figure be directly interpreted as the total data volume for a system managing 500 or more machines.
In practice, the number of managed machines and the scale of high-frequency raw data processing are two distinct metrics.
The managed equipment scale describes how many machines the system can connect to or manage. The high-frequency data processing scale depends on the number of machines actually using high-frequency sampling, the number of channels per machine, sampling rates, and data retention policies.
Consequently, a system managing more than 500 machines does not necessarily receive continuous raw waveforms from every machine at the same sampling frequency. When describing system scale, these two figures should not be conflated.
Signal Processing Pipeline The data pipeline can be divided into four stages:
Raw data acquisition: Capture sensor signals such as vibration, current, and pressure while handling timestamps, missing values, and data quality issues. Windowing: Divide continuous signals into fixed-length data windows. Window length and overlap ratio are configured according to equipment characteristics and analytical requirements. Feature extraction: Apply FFT, wavelet transforms, and statistical methods to calculate features such as RMS, spectral entropy, and energy within specific frequency bands. Feature output: Convert the results into fixed-format feature vectors for downstream anomaly detection and equipment health models. For example, a model might consume a 64-dimensional feature vector instead of receiving the complete raw waveform every time. This can reduce computational overhead in downstream processing, although its suitability depends on the anomaly patterns and model requirements. If feature extraction discards important information, downstream models cannot recover it.
Edge Performance Optimization Several optimization strategies can be applied at this layer:
Process data in batches or windows to reduce the overhead of handling individual samples. Use preallocated ring buffers to reduce the frequency of memory allocation and data copying. Separate high-frequency signal processing from lower-frequency equipment state analysis. Apply different retention and transmission policies to raw data, extracted features, and event data instead of treating all data identically. Continuously monitor queue lengths, data loss rates, CPU utilization, and end-to-end latency. The original presentation reported the following performance comparisons:
Processing latency decreased from 45 ms to below 12 ms. CPU utilization decreased from 100% to 32%. Throughput increased by approximately 2.5 times. Reducing latency from 45 ms to below 12 ms represents a latency reduction of at least approximately 73.3%.
However, latency and throughput are different metrics. The throughput improvement cannot be derived directly from the latency reduction. A meaningful throughput comparison requires measuring the amount of data actually processed per unit of time under identical or comparable input loads.
CPU utilization must also be interpreted in the context of the measurement interval, core count, and test workload. The original figures of 100% and 32% are retained here as comparisons reported in the existing presentation. Without access to the original test records, they should not be interpreted as steady-state utilization levels that apply to every deployment environment.
04. Two-Stage Anomaly Detection Equipment failure datasets are typically highly imbalanced. Normal operating data is relatively easy to collect, while actual failure cases are comparatively rare. As a result, purely supervised learning approaches often face a shortage of labeled failure data.
False alarms present another practical challenge. Even if a model can identify certain anomalies, generating large numbers of alerts that do not lead to actionable responses can undermine the confidence of on-site personnel.
This architecture therefore adopts a layered detection strategy that separates lightweight initial screening from more detailed anomaly assessment.
Stage 1: Rapid Screening Isolation Forest can identify samples that differ from the distribution of previously observed data. Because it is relatively lightweight, it can be suitable for some resource-constrained edge environments.
The objective of the first stage is to quickly identify data that warrants further investigation, rather than automatically interpreting every anomaly score as evidence of equipment failure.
Stage 2: In-Depth Assessment An Autoencoder can evaluate differences between incoming data and learned normal operating patterns through reconstruction error.
In practice, thresholds can be configured according to equipment type, operating state, and sensor channel. This helps prevent normal process transitions or load variations from being indiscriminately classified as failures.
Alert Consolidation and Suppression Alert management should not depend solely on model outputs. The system should also consider:
Repeated alerts from the same machine within a short period. Alert duration and anomaly severity. The machine’s current operating mode and maintenance status. Whether an alert has already been acknowledged or associated with a maintenance work order. For example, the system could apply a five-minute duplicate-alert suppression window for the same equipment and anomaly type.
However, this mechanism must preserve exceptions for severity escalation and safety-related events. Reducing notifications must never conceal emerging risks.
The original presentation reported the following metrics:
The false-positive rate decreased from 15% to 3.2%. The F1-score reached 0.94. The average fault detection time decreased by 40%. These metrics describe different aspects of system performance.
False-positive rate: The evaluation must first establish whether this refers to the proportion of normal samples incorrectly classified as anomalous (False Positive Rate, FPR) or the proportion of alerts that are false alarms. These metrics have different denominators and are not interchangeable. F1-score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. It helps assess the balance between these two metrics but must still be interpreted in the context of the evaluation dataset and failure categories. Fault detection time: The starting point must be clearly defined. It could be the actual onset of a failure, the first appearance of anomalous features, or the first effective alert generated by the system. Furthermore, if the reduction in false alarms resulted from a combination of model improvements, threshold tuning, and duplicate-alert suppression, the outcome should be understood as an improvement in the overall alerting workflow rather than attributed entirely to the model itself.
Because the original test data is unavailable, the figures in this article are retained as descriptions of previously reported project results. They are not presented as independently validated or universally applicable model performance benchmarks.
05. Equipment Health Management and Remaining Useful Life Prediction Anomaly detection primarily answers the question, “Is the equipment currently deviating from its normal operating condition?”
Predictive maintenance goes a step further by addressing two additional questions: “How is the equipment’s health changing over time?” and “When might maintenance be required?”
Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) typically integrates sensor features, equipment history, failure modes, and maintenance records. When sufficient data is available, a Remaining Useful Life (RUL) model can estimate how much time remains before equipment reaches a defined failure condition.
RUL Model Design Different approaches can be selected according to the available data and prediction requirements:
Statistical methods and survival analysis: Methods such as the Weibull distribution can characterize equipment failure-time distributions under appropriate assumptions. Time-series models: LSTM or Transformer architectures can analyze how equipment health indicators evolve over time. Domain-specific features: Frequency-band energy, spectral entropy, vibration amplitude, and equipment load can be combined to improve the model’s ability to recognize actual failure modes. These methods have different applicability conditions. A Weibull distribution alone does not guarantee accurate RUL predictions for an individual machine. Predicting the remaining life of a specific piece of equipment still requires appropriate observations and model validation.
From Predictions to Maintenance Planning The value of RUL is not simply the generation of a time estimate. It enables maintenance teams to plan personnel, spare parts, and equipment downtime in advance.
For example, predicted RUL can be divided into three maintenance planning intervals:
Routine monitoring: Predicted RUL exceeds 30 days. Continue monitoring equipment condition at the established frequency. Advance preparation: Predicted RUL is between 7 and 30 days. Verify spare-part availability and maintenance resources. Priority assessment: Predicted RUL is below 7 days. Arrange an engineering inspection and evaluate the maintenance schedule. These intervals are illustrative. Actual thresholds should be determined according to the consequences of equipment failure, spare-part lead times, prediction uncertainty, and production scheduling requirements.
For equipment involving safety risks, decisions about continued operation must not rely solely on the RUL estimate.
The original presentation reported the following metrics:
RUL prediction RMSE of no more than 32 hours. A 42% reduction in unplanned downtime. A 28% reduction in maintenance costs. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) measures the overall error between predicted and actual values. It is calculated as follows:
$$ \mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2} $$where \(\hat{y}_i\) represents the predicted value and \(y_i\) represents the actual value.
RMSE gives greater weight to larger prediction errors. Therefore, an RMSE of no more than 32 hours does not mean that every individual prediction is guaranteed to be within 32 hours of the actual value.
RUL evaluation must also account for the prediction time, equipment type, failure definition, and evaluation dataset selection methodology. Results from different equipment types or failure modes should not be combined or compared without considering these differences.
The reported reductions of 42% in unplanned downtime and 28% in maintenance costs should likewise be treated as overall improvement metrics within a specific project scope. If the contributions of the AI model cannot be separated from changes in maintenance workflows, spare-parts strategies, equipment upgrades, or other operational factors, the entire improvement should not be attributed directly to the AI model.
06. Edge Deployment and Model Lifecycle Management Once a model has been trained, another critical challenge remains: how can it be deployed reliably across different devices and production lines, while ensuring that the existing service can be restored if an update fails?
In a factory environment, deployment involves much more than packaging an application into a container. The operating system, hardware architecture, device drivers, inference engine versions, and equipment communication protocols can all affect whether a model runs correctly.
A robust deployment workflow can therefore be divided into the following stages.
1. Standardized Packaging Package the model, inference application, dependencies, and configuration files into a versioned and traceable release artifact. Compatibility testing should also be performed for different hardware platforms.
2. Shadow Deployment Run the new model alongside the current model or existing rule-based system without allowing it to directly affect production control decisions.
Compare output differences, inference latency, resource utilization, and representative failure cases to determine whether the new version meets the requirements for production deployment.
Shadow deployment should cover a representative range of equipment operating conditions. Two weeks may serve as a reference period, but it may not be sufficient or appropriate for equipment where failures are rare.
3. Canary Release Deploy the new version to a small subset of devices before gradually expanding deployment. For example, rollout may proceed through 5%, 20%, and finally 100% of the target fleet.
Each stage should have clearly defined acceptance criteria and thresholds that must be satisfied before proceeding.
4. Monitoring and Rollback Continuously monitor inference failure rates, latency, resource utilization, and the distribution of model outputs.
If any metric exceeds its predefined threshold, the system should stop expanding the rollout and follow an established procedure to revert to a previously validated version.
On top of this workflow, a self-service management interface can be provided for production engineers. Depending on their access permissions, users can select model versions, inspect deployment status, and initiate rollbacks without directly modifying internal model parameters.
The original presentation lists several project metrics:
Container image size below 300 MB. Cold-start time below 30 seconds. Deployment cycle reduced from six months to two weeks. These figures should be interpreted with clearly defined measurement boundaries. Container image size should distinguish between an individual service image and the complete runtime environment. Cold-start time should separately account for container startup, model loading, and the time required for the service to become ready.
The deployment cycle also needs a clearly defined start and end point. For example, it could measure the time from candidate release readiness to production deployment, or the entire process from initial requirements to a completed production rollout.
These figures can be retained as project-specific targets from the original material, but they should not be treated as universal benchmarks that every edge device can achieve.
07. Edge Agent: Task Orchestration and Decision Boundaries The role of an Edge Agent is to integrate sensor data, model inference, equipment states, and maintenance procedures into an executable and traceable workflow.
An Edge Agent does not necessarily need to invoke a large language model for every decision. For tasks with strict latency requirements and well-defined inputs and outputs, conventional program logic or lightweight models are often easier to test and validate.
An Agent is better suited to tasks involving cross-tool coordination, information integration, or multi-step execution.
Task Allocation at the Edge Within this architecture, responsibilities can be divided into three categories:
Real-time signal processing: Perform data acquisition, feature extraction, and necessary low-latency inference at the edge. State assessment and task orchestration: Combine anomaly scores, Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimates, equipment states, and maintenance records to determine whether further inspection is needed or a maintenance work order should be created. Equipment control and safety handling: Execute control actions through systems with explicit control logic and validated safety mechanisms. Free-form generated text or unvalidated model outputs must never be translated directly into high-risk control commands. Workflow frameworks such as LangGraph can help manage Agent state, tool calls, retries, and execution branches. A Model Router can select an appropriate model or rule engine based on task complexity, latency requirements, and available computing resources.
However, adopting these frameworks does not automatically guarantee real-time performance or safety. Execution time, error handling, resource constraints, and exceptional execution paths must still be tested and validated.
Handling Network Disconnections Edge systems must account for network outages, unavailable centralized services, and model-serving failures.
A reasonable design ensures that essential monitoring and local state-assessment functions can continue operating according to predefined rules when upstream connectivity is lost. If the system cannot reliably determine its own state, it should enter a predefined degraded operating mode.
However, degraded operation does not mean that every device should take the same action. Some equipment may need to reduce its operating load, while other devices may need to stop specific operations or hand control back to an existing controller.
The appropriate response must be determined through equipment-specific risk analysis and safety engineering, rather than inferred autonomously by a general-purpose Agent.
Three concepts must be distinguished:
Offline service availability: Whether the edge system can continue performing its designated local monitoring or inference tasks during a network outage. Task execution success rate: Whether the Agent can complete tool calls, state updates, maintenance work-order creation, and other workflow steps. Equipment safety: Whether existing controllers and safety mechanisms continue to protect the equipment during communication failures, model anomalies, or task execution errors. These concepts require different evaluation methods. An Agent’s task success rate cannot substitute for equipment safety validation.
The original presentation proposes a command round-trip latency below 20 ms and offline autonomous operation availability of 99.5%.
For command latency, the measurement boundaries must be explicitly defined, including whether network transmission, model inference, and tool execution are included. Offline availability also requires a defined measurement period, a description of the offline scenarios being evaluated, and clear criteria for determining whether the service is available.
For OHT systems, transport platforms, and other high-risk equipment, safety must continue to rely on independent safety mechanisms and appropriate verification procedures. Agent execution success alone is not sufficient evidence of equipment safety.
08. Industrial RAG: Making Equipment Knowledge Searchable and Traceable Knowledge in a factory exists in more than equipment manuals. It is also scattered across maintenance logs, fault analysis reports, engineering notes, and historical work orders.
These sources often have inconsistent formats, naming conventions, and data quality. Simply placing documents into a vector database may produce fluent answers, but fluent answers are not necessarily correct or applicable to the equipment’s current operating conditions.
The primary objective of Industrial Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is therefore not merely to generate answers. It is to establish a traceable workflow connecting user questions, retrieved evidence, and original source documents.
Knowledge Processing Pipeline Document preparation and access control: Convert document formats, remove duplicates, identify versions, and handle sensitive information while preserving document provenance and access permissions. Semantic chunking and indexing: Divide documents into appropriate text chunks based on their structure and content, then generate vector representations. Hybrid retrieval: Combine BM25 keyword search, vector retrieval, and metadata filtering to reduce retrieval problems caused by technical terminology, equipment identifiers, and similar documents. Reranking: Use a reranker to reassess the relevance of candidate documents to the user’s question. Answer generation and citations: Generate answers based on retrieved evidence and provide references to original documents, versions, and page numbers so that users can verify the information. Constraints in Enterprise Environments Deploying RAG in a factory requires careful consideration of whether document-level permissions are enforced in retrieval results, whether the model can access unauthorized information, and how the system handles conflicting or outdated documents.
For equipment maintenance recommendations, answers should clearly distinguish between information explicitly documented in the source material and inferences generated by the model.
If sufficient evidence cannot be found, the system should be allowed to respond that the available information is insufficient, rather than inventing additional operating procedures merely to provide a complete-looking answer.
Document indexes and query logs should also have retention periods, auditing procedures, and access permissions appropriate to the sensitivity of the underlying data.
The original presentation lists the following scale and performance metrics:
850,000 documents. More than 20,000 queries per month. Knowledge lookup time reduced from an average of three hours to 40 seconds. When interpreting these figures, document counts should distinguish between original documents, document versions, and indexed chunks created through document segmentation. Query volume should distinguish between submitted requests and requests that successfully retrieve useful answers.
Knowledge lookup time should be defined as the time from a user’s question to the identification of a relevant knowledge source. It should not automatically be equated with the time required to complete an entire troubleshooting or maintenance procedure.
If the original three-hour and 40-second figures were calculated using different measurement criteria, they should not be directly compared as equivalent metrics.
Because the historical test records are not currently available for re-examination, the figures from the original material are retained without making additional assumptions about their measurement methodology or treating them as guaranteed results for all RAG systems.
09. MLOps: Continuous Monitoring After Model Deployment Good performance on test data does not guarantee that a model will maintain the same quality after deployment.
Equipment may experience changes in component condition, maintenance activities, operating loads, or process conditions. These changes can produce data distributions that differ from the training data.
Consequently, deployed models require continuous monitoring and a complete workflow that connects issue detection, model evaluation, and version updates.
Drift Monitoring Depending on the characteristics of the data, metrics such as the Population Stability Index (PSI), the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test, or other distribution-difference measures can be used to identify deviations from an established baseline.
For example, a PSI value above 0.25 may serve as a warning threshold in certain scenarios. However, exceeding this threshold does not automatically mean that the model has failed.
Thresholds should be determined based on data distributions, feature characteristics, and actual validation results.
The monitoring system should also track missing data, sensor abnormalities, inference latency, and model output distributions. This helps prevent sensor failures from being incorrectly classified as model drift.
If a seven-day rolling baseline is used to track equipment conditions, care must be taken to prevent the baseline from continuously absorbing slowly developing anomalies.
A more robust approach is to establish dynamic baselines based on equipment operating modes and historical data, supported by anomaly-state checks and explicit baseline-update conditions. This reduces the risk of incorporating persistent faults into the definition of normal behavior.
Model Update Workflow A more complete MLOps workflow may include the following steps:
Periodically evaluate data quality and model performance. Develop candidate models to address confirmed issues. Validate candidates against historical data and relevant simulated scenarios. Compare new and existing versions in shadow mode. Release validated versions incrementally after the required reviews. Preserve version information, data provenance, parameters, and validation records for traceability and rollback. The purpose of automation is not to replace a model immediately whenever drift is detected. Instead, it is to shorten the time required to detect problems, evaluate candidate models, and deploy updates while keeping the process controlled and auditable.
The original presentation lists the following metrics:
Automatic retraining cycle reduced from two months to two weeks. Abnormal equipment downtime reduced by 75%. 1,200 hours of manual effort saved annually. The automatic retraining cycle should distinguish among data updates, model training, model validation, and production deployment. Increasing retraining frequency does not necessarily improve model quality; every candidate model must still satisfy the required validation criteria.
Abnormal downtime and manual effort are system-level or process-level metrics. If improvements also result from changes to data pipelines, automation tools, maintenance workflows, or workforce responsibilities, the entire benefit should not be attributed directly to the model retraining mechanism.
10. System Integration and Future Development Directions The components discussed in the preceding sections—stream processing, anomaly detection, RUL prediction, Edge Agents, Industrial RAG, and MLOps—address different layers of the overall system.
Stream processing ensures that data can be acquired and analyzed reliably. Anomaly detection and RUL models provide evidence for equipment condition assessment. Agents integrate information and coordinate tasks. RAG provides traceable document-based knowledge. MLOps manages the model lifecycle from validation through production deployment and ongoing operation.
These components must be integrated through clearly defined data interfaces, access-control mechanisms, and error-handling procedures. Simply connecting multiple services does not automatically create an autonomous decision-making system.
Version 1.0: Establishing an Observable, Predictable, and Maintainable Foundation The first phase focuses on ensuring that every component has well-defined inputs and outputs, measurable monitoring indicators, and appropriate failure-handling procedures. Performance should then be validated on a limited number of devices and production lines.
System Phase 1 Focus Evaluation Metrics Real-time streaming platform Establish data acquisition and feature-processing pipelines Throughput, data loss rate, end-to-end latency Anomaly detection Reduce invalid alerts while preserving important events False positive rate, false negative rate, F1 score RUL prediction Estimate equipment health and remaining useful life RMSE, prediction intervals, maintenance decision effectiveness Edge Agent Coordinate models, tools, and maintenance workflows Task success rate, latency, failure recovery capability Industrial RAG Establish document retrieval and answer traceability Retrieval quality, answer correctness, citation traceability MLOps Establish model versioning and release workflows Deployment cycle, rollback time, version traceability completeness Version 2.0: From Individual Equipment Analytics to Cross-Equipment Collaboration Once data processing, model quality, and deployment workflows are stable for individual devices, the system can begin exploring collaboration across multiple devices and production lines.
Potential development directions include:
Extending real-time data processing to more devices while evaluating the bandwidth and computational requirements associated with higher sampling frequencies. Combining information from multiple sensors to improve the detection of complex, multi-factor anomalies. Integrating RUL estimates with spare-parts management, maintenance scheduling, and work-order systems. Building an equipment knowledge graph to support relationship-based queries across documents and devices. Enabling different Edge Agents to exchange equipment states and task results within their authorized access boundaries. In the longer term, an Edge Agent Swarm architecture could be explored, in which multiple edge agents collaborate to handle different devices or tasks.
However, multi-agent collaboration introduces additional challenges, including state consistency, task conflicts, communication failures, access control, and error propagation.
Before expanding autonomous collaboration, the responsibilities of each Agent, its permitted actions, and its failure-handling procedures must be explicitly defined.
11. Conclusion Building an Edge-AI system for a smart factory requires much more than combining sensors, machine learning models, and an Agent framework.
The real challenge lies in engineering the entire system: ensuring reliable data acquisition, running models within constrained computing resources, determining whether anomaly results are trustworthy, recovering safely from deployment failures, and integrating AI recommendations into equipment operations and maintenance workflows without compromising existing safety mechanisms.
From this perspective, predictive maintenance and autonomous decision agents are not two independent capabilities.
Predictive maintenance provides equipment condition assessments and risk information. The Agent translates that information into traceable workflows. Data governance, model monitoring, and safety controls provide the essential foundation for keeping the entire system reliable over the long term.
For organizations seeking to advance these systems, the priority should not be achieving full autonomy from the outset. Instead, each component should first become observable, verifiable, and recoverable. The scope of AI-assisted decision-making can then be expanded incrementally.
This is the central design principle behind this architecture: AI capabilities and system responsibility boundaries must be clearly defined together for the technology to operate reliably on the factory floor.

summary:
TL;DR

  • The architecture spans six layers, from sensors and streaming through PHM, edge agents, and MES/EAP safety integration.
  • A 20-machine, 3-channel, 2 kHz example generates about 41.5 GB/day of raw data; managed fleet size and high-frequency stream scale are separate metrics.
  • Detection uses a two-stage pipeline: Isolation Forest screening followed by Autoencoder assessment, with alert consolidation to reduce noise.
  • RUL prediction (Weibull, LSTM/Transformer, domain features) feeds 30-day and 7-day maintenance planning; the reported figures are project-specific, not universal benchmarks.
  • Models move through standardized packaging, shadow deployment, canary rollout (5% → 20% → 100%), monitoring, and rollback.
  • Edge Agents, Industrial RAG, and MLOps connect evidence and workflows, but safety-critical control stays outside the LLM.

Bottom line: Make each layer observable, verifiable, and recoverable before expanding autonomous decision-making.
title: Smart Fab Edge-AI: Predictive Maintenance and Autonomous Decision Agent System
